questions.stem: A nurse who is off duty voluntarily provides basic first aid at a roadside crash and later asks whether a Good Samaritan law guarantees immunity from liability. Which explanation is most accurate for a national NCLEX-style question?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Because the nurse was off duty, every U.S. jurisdiction automatically grants complete immunity for interventions performed during an emergency, even outside usual competence.","B":"Professional licensure creates a nationwide legal duty to stop at every emergency, and failure to provide care is automatically professional negligence.","C":"Legal protections and duties vary by jurisdiction; a nurse should not assume blanket immunity and should provide reasonable care within competence and applicable law.","D":"Accepting no payment converts the encounter into a federal Good Samaritan case, so state law and the reasonableness of the care no longer matter in liability review."}}
questions.rationale: Good Samaritan protections are not a single nationwide blanket immunity. The common-law Good Samaritan rule recognizes that a person who voluntarily undertakes care assumes a duty to use reasonable care, while statutory protections and duties can vary by jurisdiction. A national exam item should therefore avoid promising universal immunity and emphasize reasonable, competent care under applicable law.
questions.source_name: Cornell Legal Information Institute — Good Samaritan Rule; NCSBN — State Nurse Practice Acts
questions.source_detail: Common-law Good Samaritan principles require reasonable care after voluntarily undertaking assistance; nursing practice requirements are jurisdiction-specific.

questions.stem: A nurse reports a safety concern to a regulatory agency and is then reassigned to undesirable shifts. Which statement best reflects federal whistleblower principles?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Any report by a healthcare worker automatically receives identical federal protection regardless of the applicable law, subject, reporting method, or context now.","B":"A schedule change cannot qualify as retaliation because only termination or a reduction in salary is considered an adverse employment action.","C":"The nurse must first resign before a retaliation complaint can be evaluated because continued employment prevents proof of an adverse action.","D":"A reassignment may be retaliatory if it follows activity protected by an applicable whistleblower law; the specific protection depends on the governing statute."}}
questions.rationale: OSHA explains that whistleblower protection depends on protected activity under an applicable law. Adverse actions can include reassignment, discipline, reduced hours, demotion, firing, or other actions that would deter a reasonable employee from raising concerns. Protection is therefore not automatic for every report; the relevant statute and facts matter.
questions.source_detail: Protected activities and retaliation standards vary by the specific whistleblower law; reassignment can be an adverse action.

questions.stem: A hospitalized client will probably need home oxygen, medication teaching, and follow-up services after discharge. Which approach best reflects CMS discharge-planning requirements?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Delay assessment of post-hospital needs until a discharge date is fixed so the plan reflects only services that can be arranged on the final day.","B":"Evaluate likely post-hospital service and self-care needs early enough to develop and implement a safe transition plan without unnecessary discharge delay.","C":"Limit discharge planning to clients who personally request it because hospitals are not responsible for evaluating transition needs unless asked.","D":"Complete discharge planning after the client leaves the hospital so community providers can determine which services are necessary and then notify the hospital."}}
questions.rationale: CMS hospital discharge-planning requirements call for evaluation of the likelihood that a patient will need post-hospital services and the patient's capacity for self-care or care in the prior environment. The process must support an effective transition rather than being deferred until after discharge or restricted only to patient-requested planning.
questions.source_detail: Discharge planning evaluation includes likely post-hospital service needs and capacity for self-care or care in the prior environment.

questions.stem: During an event review, one nurse makes an unintended selection error despite following the normal process; another knowingly bypasses a required safety step despite understanding the substantial risk. Which response best reflects Just Culture?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Examine system factors and support the nurse who made a human error, while addressing the conscious high-risk violation according to its reckless-behavior classification.","B":"Apply the same disciplinary action to both nurses because outcome severity, rather than behavioral choice or system design, determines the appropriate response.","C":"Avoid individual accountability in both cases because Just Culture treats every unsafe event as a system problem regardless of deliberate behavioral choices.","D":"Discipline the inadvertent error more severely because mistakes reveal lack of competence, while treating the deliberate safety bypass as at-risk behavior needing coaching."}}
questions.rationale: AHRQ Just Culture materials distinguish human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior. Human error calls for support and system improvement; at-risk behavior calls for coaching and risk reduction; reckless behavior reflects conscious disregard of a substantial and unjustifiable risk and may warrant remedial or punitive action after fair review.
questions.source_name: AHRQ — Just Culture / Understanding Risk and Human Behavior
questions.source_detail: Human error, at-risk behavior, and reckless behavior require different responses; reckless behavior is conscious disregard of substantial unjustifiable risk.

questions.stem: A client with diabetes says the standard meal schedule conflicts with religious practices and asks to discuss safe alternatives. Which nursing action best demonstrates the QSEN competency of patient-centered care?
questions.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"Enter the standard meal schedule into the electronic record and explain that accurate documentation is the primary goal of the care plan.","B":"Use current nutrition research to choose a different meal schedule independently, without discussing the client's preferences or values before changing care.","C":"Explore the client's preferences and goals, then collaborate on a safe plan that respects those values while coordinating appropriate clinical guidance.","D":"Audit unit glucose outcomes for several months and present the aggregate data to leadership before making any individualized change to the client's plan."}}
questions.rationale: QSEN defines patient-centered care as recognizing the patient or designee as a source of control and a full partner in compassionate, coordinated care based on respect for preferences, values, and needs. Evidence, informatics, and quality improvement are also QSEN competencies, but the scenario specifically tests partnership with the individual client.
questions.source_detail: Patient-centered care emphasizes partnership and respect for patient preferences, values, and needs.
